newsitem.title: USA: N.J. man goes to court in "Megan's Law" trial.
newsitem.headline: N.J. man goes to court in "Megan's Law" trial.

text.p: Jesse Timmendequas, whose alleged rape and murder of a 7-year-old girl led to "Megan's Law" and sparked a nationwide drive to tighten supervision of sex offenders, goes on trial in New Jersey Monday.

Prosecutors say that in July 1994 twice convicted sex offender Timmendequas, 35, was living in Hamilton Township -- a working-class suburb of Trenton -- with his past unknown to his neighbours when he lured Megan Kanka into his home to see a puppy, then raped her and strangled her.
The girl's body was found in a county park, two miles away, after a two-day search.

The jury selection process was laborious, complicated by the highly public campaign to change the law in New Jersey -- and other states afterward -- led by the girl's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka. During that campaign, the criminal record of her accused killer was widely discussed.
A federal law also was enacted, giving states an incentive to pass similar restrictions.

Megan's Law requires sex offenders to register with police and empowers prosecutors to screen them for risk to the public with the public being told about those assessed as posing the highest risk. The public notification is under legal challenge in the federal courts.
The defence said the extensive publicity linking the crime to the political campaign made it necessary to screen jurors for knowledge of the new law.

Jurors were asked in a 36-page questionnaire and were quizzed in court on how much they knew about these events. Jurors were selected from semi-rural Hunterdon County to lessen the chance pre-trial publicity would taint the trial.
When the trial begins, the 12 jurors and four alternates will be bused the 20 miles between Flemington and the Mercer County Court in Trenton, the state capital.
Megan's Law was in legal limbo. A series of rulings left the state empowered to require offenders to register and to consider offender appeals, but not to notify the public.
A federal court is considering an appeal. Alexander Artway, the sex offender making the appeal, had not been notified by the state of its intention to publish his name and record to neighbours.

Judge Nicholas Politan had ruled earlier that the state law would impose unconstitutional extra punishment if it were applied to any person whose crime was committed before Oct. 31, 1994, the day it took effect.
Politan ruled that such offenders cannot be exposed to the public, calling it an ex post facto punishment. An appeals court has yet to rule on the merits of the ruling.
